title: Procedural Record
description:
CoALA procedural memory: how to do something. Learned routines, playbooks, and heuristics.

Deliberate narrowing of CoALA: the paper's procedural memory includes the agent's own code, and the authors flag rewriting it as the riskiest learning modality. This agent stores procedures as DATA that a host reads and chooses to follow — never as executable code, and never applied to itself. Every procedural write is additionally gated behind human approval before it becomes retrievable.

trigger.description: The condition under which this procedure applies. Recall matches a query against this first — a procedure retrieved in the wrong situation is worse than no procedure at all.

preconditions.description: What must already be true before the steps are safe to run. A host that cannot verify a precondition should not run the procedure.

steps.description: Ordered instructions in natural language. Instructions, not code: the host decides how to carry each one out.

tool.description: Suggested tool, if the procedure was learned in a context that had one. Advisory only — the host is not obliged to have it.

on_failure.description: What to do if this step fails, e.g. 'skip', 'abort', or a natural-language fallback.

success_signal.description: How a host knows the procedure worked. Without this the usage counters below are unfalsifiable.

approval.description:
The gate. A procedural record is invisible to recall until state is 'approved'.

`reviewed_by` is a claim, not proof — a string any caller could write. The proof is `signature`: an Ed25519 signature by a key the reviewer holds and the server never sees the private half of. An agent cannot manufacture one, which is what turns the gate from a convention into a control. It is required whenever state is 'approved' or 'rejected'.

reviewed_by.description: Identifier of the human who decided. Must match the `reviewer:` line inside the signed payload, and must be absent while state is 'pending'.

rationale.description: Why it was approved or rejected. Rejections are kept, not deleted: a rejected candidate that keeps being re-proposed is a signal about the proposer.

reviewed_by.description: Narrowed from the nullable form above: a decided record must name a reviewer. Requiring only presence would let `reviewed_by: null` through, which is an approval nobody made.

usage.description: Whether the learned procedure actually works in practice. A procedure with many invocations and few successes should be revised or retired — this is the feedback loop that keeps procedural memory honest.

supersedes.description: Prior procedure this one replaces. Revision is normal; the old version is marked superseded rather than deleted so a regression can be traced.

approval_signature.title: Approval Signature
approval_signature.description:
Proof that a specific human made this decision about this exact candidate.

The signed payload is stored VERBATIM rather than reconstructed at verification time. That is the whole point: years later, with nothing but this record and the reviewer's public key, anyone can re-verify the decision offline. Reconstructing the payload from current field values would instead prove only that the fields are self-consistent — which is not evidence of anything.

alg.description: Only Ed25519 in v1. Named explicitly so a future algorithm can be added without ambiguity about how old signatures were made.

key_id.description: SHA256 fingerprint of the signing public key, OpenSSH style: 'SHA256:' + unpadded base64 of the digest of the 32 raw public key bytes. Identifies which reviewer key to verify against, and survives key rotation — a retired key stays in policy so its old signatures keep verifying.

signed_payload.description:
The exact UTF-8 byte string that was signed, stored as-is. Fixed-field and newline-delimited, never JSON — canonical JSON is a footgun (key order, unicode escaping, number formatting) and a verifier that has to re-serialise can disagree with the signer.

Format, in this order, each line terminated by \n:
  memory-agent-approval-v2
  scope: <scope>
  proposal: <proposal_id>
  candidate_sha256: <hex>
  decision: approve|reject
  reviewer: <reviewer_id>
  nonce: <server-issued nonce>
  expires: <RFC3339>

sig.description: Base64 of the 64-byte Ed25519 signature over signed_payload.

candidate_sha256.description:
SHA256 of the candidate at signing time, lowercase hex. Also appears inside signed_payload; duplicated here so a tamper check is an index lookup rather than a string parse. If this stops matching the stored record, the procedure was altered after approval and must be treated as unapproved.

Exactly what is hashed, because a verifier that disagrees here rejects valid approvals: the proposal's `candidate` object serialised as UTF-8 JSON with keys sorted lexicographically, no insignificant whitespace (`,` and `:` separators), and non-ASCII characters left unescaped. In Python: `json.dumps(candidate, sort_keys=True, separators=(',', ':'), ensure_ascii=False).encode()`. The hash covers the candidate only — never the envelope fields the server assigns, which would make it unreproducible.

The covered keys are exactly `content`, `trigger`, `preconditions`, `steps`, `success_signal` and `failure_signal`. `content` is covered deliberately and must stay covered: it is the only indexed field and the text `memory_recall` returns, so it is what an agent actually follows. A signature that omitted it would let an approved procedure's instructions be rewritten without invalidating the signature, leaving `verify` reporting success on a procedure nobody approved. Not yet covered: `supersedes` and `evidence_record_ids`.

verified_at.description: When the server last checked the signature. Re-verification is cheap and the daemon does it on a sweep, so a record whose content drifted from its signature gets caught rather than trusted indefinitely.
